title: The Hunting Party
full_review:
Richard Gere follows up his semifictional turn as author and con man Clifford Irving in "The Hoax" with another fanciful yarn based, as they say, on actual events.

"The Hunting Party" (MGM/Weinstein), a sometimes interesting though uneven black comedy, finds him playing Simon Hunt, a washed-up broadcast journalist who's been toiling in obscurity since a breakdown years earlier while covering the Bosnian war.

A surprise reunion with his old buddy and former cameraman Duck (Terrence Howard), who comes to the region on assignment, leads Simon to suggest he has a lead for the story of a lifetime: an exclusive interview with a notorious war criminal who has thus far eluded international search efforts in and around Sarajevo. He claims his contact has put him onto the whereabouts of the fictitious Boghanovic, aka "the Fox."

Benjamin (Jesse Eisenberg), a nerdy cub reporter and the son of a network executive, insists on tagging along, and the unlikely trio sets out to find their quarry, for Simon reveals they will actually capture him.

The film was adapted from journalist Scott Anderson's Esquire magazine article, "What I Did on My Summer Vacation," which related how Anderson and four other journalists, all alumni of covering the Balkans, returned to Sarajevo in 2000 and decided to apprehend war criminal Radovan Karadicz. During their mission, local authorities mistook them for CIA agents, a mix-up replicated in the film.

Writer-director Richard Shepard's brew of drama and black comedy works sometimes, but not enough of the time, and despite individual pluses and an implicitly strong indictment of governmental inaction (for example, the United Nations, the CIA and the European Union) in capturing war criminals, overall it fails to convince.

The film contains much gratuitous rough language and profanity; crass expressions; rear and upper female nudity; some violence including torture; a fox hunt; sexual references; brief nongraphic scene of sexuality; and premarital situations. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
